title: SEMICON India 2026: New Delhi Pushes to Localise Chip Materials and Gases
excerpt: At the fifth SEMICON India summit in New Delhi, officials brokered roundtables with suppliers from the US, Japan and South Korea while Merck, Applied Materials and Lam Research announced India supply-chain commitments under the ₹1.275 lakh crore Semicon 2.0 programme.
body:
• At SEMICON India 2026 in New Delhi, the government's focus has shifted from winning fabrication projects to building the domestic supply chain beneath them — local suppliers of materials, gases, chemicals, equipment sub-systems and design IP.
  • The Centre is running targeted matchmaking roundtables between Indian manufacturers and suppliers from the US, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Malaysia and Europe during the Sept. 17-19 summit.
  • Merck, Applied Materials, Lam Research and ASML all made India supply-chain announcements on day one, including Applied Materials' $5 billion "India Vision 2035" and Lam's roughly Rs 100 billion silicon-component plant.
  • Semicon 2.0, approved in July with a ₹1.275 lakh crore outlay, formalises the shift: six pillars covering design, equipment and materials, fabs, advanced packaging, R&D and talent.

India's semiconductor strategy is moving down the stack. At SEMICON India 2026, which Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurated on Thursday at Yashobhoomi in New Delhi, the government's message was that the next phase of the mission is not about landing another fabrication plant — it is about localising the materials, gases, chemicals and equipment that fabs need to run.

The government is using the three-day summit to broker industrial partnerships between Indian companies and overseas suppliers across semiconductor materials, components, manufacturing equipment and intellectual property, officials said, according to Communications Today. The Centre has identified Indian manufacturers of equipment, sub-assemblies and components for targeted roundtable discussions with counterparts from the US, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Malaysia and Europe — an effort aimed at integrating domestic suppliers into global semiconductor value chains.

The fifth edition of SEMICON India, themed "Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem," runs September 17-19 and brings together more than 500 exhibitors — including 294 international companies — from over 40 countries, with more than 150 speakers across tracks covering manufacturing, chemicals, gases and materials, supply chains, design and talent.

Day One Announcements

The summit opened with a string of supply-chain commitments. Merck's CEO of electronics said fab viability requires parallel local investment in ultra-pure semiconductor chemicals and gases, safe materials handling and certified domestic suppliers. Applied Materials' president of SPG announced "India Vision 2035": $5 billion in investment over the next decade and a tenfold expansion of its India-based supply-chain capacity by 2035, according to Indian Infrastructure's report from the event.

Lam Research's chief operating officer announced roughly Rs 100 billion for the company's first silicon-component manufacturing and vertical ingot-processing plant in India, and said its Semiverse university programme has now reached more than 99 universities. ASML's executive vice president reiterated the company's partnership with Tata Electronics for lithography solutions at the Dholera fab and said ASML is considering integrating Indian suppliers into its global supply chain.

The Indian Economic Observer reported Rs 1 lakh crore in investment commitments, 16 MoUs and five other announcements on day one. Tata Electronics signed a string of agreements: with Fujifilm Corporation and JSR Corporation on localisation and supply of critical semiconductor materials and advanced chemicals; with Nexperia on wafer manufacturing, assembly and testing; with Ascendas First Space on a 363-acre vendor park in Dholera, Gujarat, to support suppliers around its fabrication facility; with BESI Singapore on advanced packaging; and with Semiconductor Laboratory on design services, process technology, supply-chain localisation and talent development. Kaynes Semicon signed agreements with OptoML India, GridCrest Technologies and Sensesemi covering advanced packaging and assembly and testing.

Modi also virtually inaugurated commercial production lines at CDIL Semiconductor in Mohali for discrete devices and Suchi Semicon in Surat for packaging — bringing the count to five operational commercial ATMP units, alongside Micron, Kaynes and CG Semi, out of twelve approved under Semicon 1.0.

Context & Background

The push sits under Semicon 2.0, approved by the Union Cabinet in July with an outlay of ₹1.275 lakh crore (about $13.5 billion, up from $8 billion under Semicon 1.0). The programme's budget expansion from $8 billion to $13.5 billion was highlighted by the Prime Minister in his inaugural address, alongside 7.8 per cent quarterly GDP growth. Union IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw laid out six pillars for the second phase: design, equipment and materials, fabs, advanced packaging, applied R&D and talent — a clear broadening from the fab-centric first phase, which trained 70,000 design engineers and deployed EDA tools across more than 500 organisations.

India's chip market has grown from about $38 billion in 2023 to an estimated $45-50 billion in 2024-25, with the government targeting $100-110 billion by 2030, according to an AFP report. The government also proposed training one lakh technicians over five years in partnership with industry and international institutions including Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute.

Impact & Analysis

The strategy reflects a hard-learned lesson from global chip building: a fab without a local supply chain is a hostage to imports. Specialty gases, photoresists, ultra-pure chemicals and precision components are where margins pool and where supply disruptions bite hardest — the pandemic-era shortages and the export-control era have both made that clear. By steering foreign partners into joint ventures and vendor parks now, while the Dholera fab and other facilities are still ramping, India is trying to avoid building fabs that depend entirely on imported inputs.

The announcements from equipment majors matter more than headline dollar figures. Applied Materials' tenfold supply-chain expansion and ASML's openness to Indian suppliers in its global chain signal that vendors see enough fab capacity coming online in India to justify localising production. The test will be whether the roundtables produce commercially viable Indian suppliers in precision components and specialty materials — or end as conference MOUs.

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian-origin engineers and executives who run significant parts of the global semiconductor industry — in equipment companies, EDA firms and chip designers across the US — Semicon 2.0's materials-and-equipment focus creates a concrete bridge: supplier partnerships, vendor-park opportunities and R&D collaboration on Indian soil, alongside the workforce programmes like the Intel-ISM "Introduction to Semiconductors" course launched this week.

What's Next

SEMICON India runs through September 19 at Yashobhoomi. The next milestones to watch: which matchmaking roundtables convert into signed joint ventures, whether the ₹1 lakh crore in day-one commitments materialise into groundbreakings, and how the government's supplier-integration push shapes the coming Semicon 2.0 incentive allocations for equipment and materials.
